title: The daughter of the furrow
hookLine: a priest asks about his mother, and a king tells where his bow, and his daughter, came from
carry: bhumi devi: the earth is a mother

lines: DID YOU SHOW MY MOTHER TO RAMA?
cards: The travelers reach Mithila, and King Janaka comes out to receive them with his priests. One is Shatananda, Janaka's chief priest. His first question to Vishvamitra isn't about the bow, or the princes, or the sacrifice.
Did you show my mother to Rama? Was she honored? Did my father come back to her?
Shatananda is Ahalya and Gautama's eldest son. Yesterday's story was his family's. And when he hears yes, she's free, they're together, he's overjoyed.
Then the king speaks of something else.

teach.b: These boys would like to see the bow, Vishvamitra says, and Janaka tells its story.

teach.h: SHIVA'S BOW, RAISED AT DAKSHA'S RITE.
teach.b: Long ago, at the great sacrifice of Daksha, Shiva was refused his share of the offerings, and in anger he raised this very bow against the gods.

They begged him to relent; he did, and gave them the bow, and the gods gave it to Devarata, an ancestor of Janaka's line. It has stayed in Mithila ever since. Then Janaka tells a second story, about his daughter.
Once, he says, I was plowing a field to prepare for a sacrifice, and out of the furrow the plow had cut, a girl rose up. I raised her as my own and named her Sita.
Sita means furrow, the line a plow cuts. She wasn't born from a womb, the text says; she came from the earth itself. That's why she's called Bhumija, daughter of the earth.
And here is the teaching under the story.

teach.h: BHUMI DEVI: THE EARTH AS MOTHER.
teach.b: Hindus honor the earth as a goddess, Bhudevi or Bhumi Devi, a mother who feeds and holds everyone. Sita is her daughter, and at the very end of the Ramayana, she goes home to her. So this isn't a humble birth.
It's the most sacred one in the story.

teach.h: A TOUCH OF THE FLOOR EACH MORNING.
teach.b: That's why many Hindus, on waking, touch the floor before stepping on it and ask Mother Earth to forgive the touch of their feet.
And Janaka has decided: only the one who can handle Shiva's bow may marry this daughter of the earth. Tomorrow, what that has cost him.

how: Hindus celebrate Sita's appearance from the earth on Sita Navami, in the month of Vaishakha, and Mithila, in today's Bihar and Nepal's Janakpur region, holds her as its own daughter. Many Hindus also greet the earth on waking with a short Sanskrit verse asking her pardon for the touch of their feet.

o: Shiva's bow, kept in Mithila since Daksha's rite
a bow Janaka made to defend his city's walls
the bow Vishvamitra gave Rama at Siddhashrama

p: the furrow, rising from the earth
the earth as goddess and mother

s: Shatananda is Ahalya and Gautama's son
his first question is whether his mother was honored.
Sita was born to Janaka's queen in the palace
Janaka found her rising from a furrow as he plowed.
in Hindu teaching, the earth is just dirt under our feet
she's Bhumi Devi, a mother; many Hindus ask her pardon before stepping on her each morning.

games.q: Janaka finds a baby girl in the furrow of a field. by Hindu teaching, what does that birth say about her?
o: she's a daughter of the earth itself, Bhumi Devi's child: the most sacred birth in the story.
she's a foundling of low birth whom Janaka took pity on.
she's a farmer's child he took in.
games.why: Sita is Bhumija, daughter of the earth. the earth is a mother in Hinduism, so this birth is holy, not humble.

practice: If you'd like, do what many Hindus do on waking: touch the floor, then your forehead or heart, and silently ask the earth's pardon for stepping on her. Then sit and feel the ground beneath you, holding you the way it held Sita.
Breathe in and feel it support you; breathe out and give your weight back to it.

wordCard.voice: Janaka's bow. The bow of Shiva, kept in Mithila since Daksha's sacrifice, and the test Janaka sets for whoever would marry Sita, the daughter of the furrow.

orig.note: Sanskrit sītā: a furrow, the line cut by a plow. Janaka's daughter, found in one.

carryVoice: Your line: bhumi devi, the earth is a mother. Sita's mother, and the floor you'll step on tomorrow. That's day five hundred seven.
